headline: Microsoft's president said AI faces fewer safety rules than milk or washing machines and called for global rules with emergency brakes and outside checks before release.
score_reason: Pool 7 kept: the BBC's own interview supports the headline, though it is one company's proposal and the BBC does not date the interview.
importance_line: The president of one of the largest AI companies asking for binding rules bears first on anyone harmed by a rogue AI system, then on regulators and governments, then on rival developers; it is a proposal made on a podcast, and the White House has so far backed voluntary pledges.
summary: The BBC reports from its Big Boss Interview podcast that Brad Smith, president of Microsoft, said milk and washing machines are more strictly regulated than AI, and called for global safety rules, among them a legal duty to tell any "victim" when a rogue AI agent (software that acts on its own) breaches their system, "emergency brakes", also called kill switches, to pause AI that gets out of control, and independent government checks before new AI is released. The BBC says this puts him at odds with President Trump, who wants the industry to regulate itself so US firms do not lose ground to Chinese rivals; Smith welcomed the voluntary AI safety pledge that tech leaders signed at the White House on 29 Sep 2026, which our 30 Sep 2026 edition carried from The Guardian, but said "I don't think it's sufficient any longer", and named the UK, with its AI Security Institute, as best placed to lead the new rules.
notes: Read the BBC article in full. Reaction to Trump's self-regulation line and to the 29 Sep White House pledge (our 30 Sep 2026 edition, The Guardian). The BBC does not give the interview date.
